citation.author: Vanderhoef, John & Matthew Thomas Payne
citation.title: Press X to Wait: The Cultural Politics of Slow Game Time in Red Dead Redemption 2

discipline: Media studies / game studies (cultural-political; discourse analysis + textual/mechanical analysis)
thesis: RDR2 unusually deploys 'slow game time' against the mainstream norm of 'hegemonic game time' (action, efficiency, optimization); whether embraced or resented, its slowness exposes the unmarked temporal regime of AAA design and neoliberal chrononormativity and transforms what would be subversive, resistant play (process, stillness, unproductive waiting) into a dominant mode of engagement in a blockbuster game.
sections: Once Upon Some Times in the West (frames RDR2 as a game about slow time; gang, Arthur, closing frontier, tuberculosis; 'cowboy sim' reception)
The Critical Potentiality of Slow Game Time (situates in game-temporality scholarship and neoliberal/gamification critique)
Slow Your Horse There, Cowboy (relocates frustration from verisimilitude to temporal rupture; introduces stasis/stillness/prolongment)
Action and Stasis (mechanics & canned animations: looting, skinning, hunting, Eagle Eye, Dead Eye)
Travel and Stillness (traversal systems: horseback, train, fast-travel gating, auto-run, stamina)
Narrative and Prolongment (109 missions, cyclical hope/defeat, slow death)
Press 'X' to Wait (conclusion; generalizes to Witcher 3 / Death Stranding; Galloway on action; contemplative play space)
concepts: radical slowness (Scully-Blaker; here made dominant rather than subversive)
deliberate friction / waiting ('Press X to wait')
the pregnant potential of a null set / unproductive play
gamification and capitalist colonization of time
readings: Drawer-by-drawer cabin search after the rival-gang killing (Figure 1) as paradigmatic stasis
Legendary grizzly-bear hunt (Ch. 2 tutorial: prints, Eagle Eye, vapor trail, bait, scripted ambush) as systematic slow time in optional activity
Dead Eye as 'hegemonic play par excellence' yet recoded by surrounding slowness; mastery-slowness distinguished from radical slowness
Opening snowbound horseback trek + Dutch's 'not any time soon' line as diegetic signal of deferral
Cyclical renewal-then-tragedy story structure as 'the false hope of meritocracy'
Arthur's tuberculosis (cough Ch.2; diagnosis Ch.5 mission 65; ~30-mission decline) as narrative refusal of economy
Fireside stillness (Figure 3) read through Galloway: still playing, software still running, redefining 'action'

game_elements.element: 'Press X' button prompts (to wait / sit / not press)
game_elements.how_treated: Title emblem; contrasted with instrumental X-presses (shoot, punch, leap); pressing X to wait or refraining 'opens a contemplative play space' free of productive ends.
game_elements.locus: Section 'Press X to Wait' (conclusion); also article title

game_elements.how_treated: Prime instance of stasis: opening every cupboard and drawer one by one, items to satchel individually, extending a pickup into 'unavoidable beats.'
Repetitive canned animations whose cumulative volume adds up to considerable wait time and invites reflection on inactivity.
Nearly every in-game action linked to canned animations leaving the player waiting for the game to 'catch up to their intentions'; core engine of slow game time.

game_elements.element: Optional side activities (fishing, treasure, legendary hunting, campfire cooking)
game_elements.how_treated: Each 'produce their own wait times'; require patience and meticulous movement, thwarting efficient resource-gathering.
Slows time, mutes color, illuminates a vapor trail of the animal's path; central to deceleration in legendary hunts.
Dramatically slows time to line up shots; looks like hegemonic play but recoded by surrounding slowness; hinge between hegemonic and slow time; not the radical slowness of slow game time.

game_elements.element: Slow horseback traversal across a 29-square-mile world
game_elements.how_treated: Primary travel mode; ~16 min to cross by horse, 3+ hours walking; designed stillness privileging cinematic vistas and journey over destination.

game_elements.element: Horse stamina system + permanent horse death
game_elements.how_treated: Sprint tempered by stamina; horse death (gunfire/falling) loses all progress and forces walking out on foot until camp/town/victim; reinforces slow tempo.
Players must dismount and walk methodically between tents/wagons in the camp hub; manufactured stillness.
Auto-guides the horse to a destination and wrests the camera for cinematic framing; explicitly 'removing agency from players' while injecting contemplative inaction.
Loops the world but restricted to tracks and schedules; aids simulation but does not greatly assuage travel time.
Warp between camp and discovered townships locked behind story missions and optional camp upgrades; some players never find it; RDR2 refuses Virilio's 'logic of acceleration.'

game_elements.element: Extended horseback NPC dialogue / exposition rides
game_elements.how_treated: Riding with companions for exposition 'sutures' mechanics to enormous narrative content; slows momentum.

game_elements.element: Camp routines as a between-missions hub
game_elements.how_treated: Camp functions as a non-mounted hub demanding methodical foot movement; fireside solitude (Figure 3) anchors the Galloway reading of stillness-as-action.
game_elements.locus: Sections 'Travel and Stillness' and conclusion; Figure 3

game_elements.element: Massive narrative scale (109 missions; 2,000-page script; 40-60 hrs)
game_elements.how_treated: Six chapters + two-part epilogue; cyclical hope/defeat; basis of 'prolongment' — slowness via an excessively extended narrative.

game_elements.element: Arthur's tuberculosis as ability-degrading narrative arc
game_elements.how_treated: Cough from Ch.2, diagnosis Ch.5 (mission 65), ~30-mission decline that occasionally hinders player actions; refuses narrative economy and any avoidance of death.

themes: temporality and pace as the game's true subject and as a politics
neoliberal/capitalist colonization of time; gamification and productivity guilt
productivity vs. process; efficiency vs. stillness; speed vs. contemplation
mastery, meritocracy, and gaming capital as the affective substrate of player resistance to slowness
gendered/normative assumptions about legitimate play and players
mortality, decline, and the closing frontier mirrored in mechanics
the paradox of a crunch-built blockbuster enacting a critique of capitalist tempo
interlocutors: Bo Ruberg (queer game time; speedrunning vs. radical slowness)
Fron, Fullerton, Morie & Pearce (hegemony of play)
Nick Dyer-Witheford & Greig de Peuter (games of empire)
Sebastian Deterding et al. / P.J. Rey / Ian Bogost (gamification)

debate_axis_positions.evidence: Repeatedly emphasizes design that removes/forecloses agency to manufacture slowness: auto-run 'removing agency,' gated/obscured fast-travel, permanent horse death forcing foot travel, canned animations making the player wait; inverts Scully-Blaker's player-side 'radical slowness' into a designed dominant mode 'not necessarily contra to the game's intentions.' Galloway's coda preserves the player as co-actor even in stillness, locating critical potential in designed constraint rather than free choice.

tensions: Critique vs. complicity: RDR2 is 'not some radical, political panacea' and is 'inextricably enmeshed' in capitalist industry/crunch labor, yet still credited with genuine critical potentiality.
Verisimilitude vs. temporality: the authors reject the popular 'too much realism' explanation and relocate frustration in temporal rupture ('reality bleeds through').
Designed slowness vs. chosen slowness: reassigning Scully-Blaker's player-initiated 'radical slowness' to design creates a strain managed by distinguishing Dead Eye's mastery-slowness.
Vocal minority vs. commercial triumph: negative player discourse conceded as 'perhaps a vocal minority' against record-breaking sales, leaning on diagnostic rather than statistical value.
